extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, and graduate students in communication
extracted.subtask_description: Framework for analyzing and explaining how multiple nested factors (from individuals to social systems) shape media content, adapted to a networked public sphere and contemporary technologies. Useful for designing studies, choosing methods, and situating content as a dependent variable in media research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual-level characteristics of newsworkers
rubrics_metrics.description: On the most microlevel, consider the personal traits of newsworkers, news values they adhere to, professional roles they take on, and other demographic features (e.g., gender, race, class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess who is being drawn to the profession, how they reflect society, and what professional values they support; examine relative autonomy, identity with organizations, and psychological-level attributes influencing decisions. Examples: typologies of journalists in China (Hassid, 2011); surveys of journalists (Weaver et al., 2007).

rubrics_metrics.name: Routines
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns of behavior and unstated rules that constitute media work (deadline and space requirements, pack journalism, Tuchman’s strategic rituals, news values and occupational norms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how routines structure workflow, invoke objectivity (quotations, balancing), enable verification, adapt to screenwork and metrics, and incorporate new values from technology culture (e.g., open source ethos). Consider changes due to monitoring audience metrics, trending, and aggregation practices (Coddington, 2015).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational-level factors
rubrics_metrics.description: How media organizations (their structure, management, ownership, internal social control) operate to produce media representations as organizational products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ethnographic observation of newsrooms or distributed/network ethnography to study how different parts of organizations maintain goals, smooth conflicts (e.g., self-censorship strategies), and adapt to digital pressures (Boczkowski; Usher). Evaluate organizational fluidity, collaboration, and emergent small-staff or hybrid forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social institution / inter-organizational field
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of relationships beyond a single organization—how media coheres with and depends on other major systemic players (state, public relations, advertising, NGOs, sources).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine structured dependencies, inter-organizational relations, and how external institutions shape content and news production (Benson, Powers). Consider advocacy organizations as producers of news and their role within the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social systems / macrosocial context
rubrics_metrics.description: Macro-level cultural, political, economic systems and national contexts that condition media work and provide the broader frame for comparing influences across countries or systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study cross-national comparisons, the role of state power, globalization, and systemic forces (e.g., Hanitzsch et al., 2010); treat social systems as conditioning relationships among levels and investigate systemic constraints or enabling structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content as the dependent variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat media content broadly as the outcome to be explained—patterns of expression, linguistic characteristics, visual dimensions, and other aesthetic attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceive content as a variable that can be linked to influences at multiple levels; be explicit about assumptions regarding content’s impartiality/veracity and validate when possible (compare to other sources). Use content analysis, big data capture (blogs, Twitter), and link content measures to organizational/individual/institutional variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gatekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: The winnowing process by which a vast amount of possible news items is reduced to published stories, operating across multiple levels (individual, routines, organization, institutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine gatekeeping as multi-locational and sequenced (Vos & Heinderycks, 2015); assess persistent homogeneity or omissions despite more decentralized production. Consider indexing, cascading activation, and how gatekeeping authority flattens or persists in networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism and occupational norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Normative values of the profession (e.g., objectivity, immediacy, investigative role) that guide practices across levels and shape identity and role perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate how professionalism operates differently at each level (Reese, 2001), how it may justify managerial instructions, and how self-censorship and role perceptions change under political/economic pressure (e.g., Hong Kong case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Networked public sphere / news ecology
rubrics_metrics.description: The conceptualization of media as a networked, ecosystem-like space where professional and citizen actors, organizations, and platforms interact and blur traditional institutional boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map interconnections and node relationships (hyperlink maps, ecosystem analyses); analyze collaborative relationships (networked journalism), aggregator roles, atomization/reassembly of story units, and how networks redistribute content creation and dissemination (Anderson; Benkler).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemblage and hybrid media systems
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that media work is an assemblage of modular units (journalists, technologies, political actors) forming shifting, loosely coupled configurations rather than fixed organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the assemblage lens to identify dynamic, transitory mediated spaces; study how hybrid systems produce political information cycles and emergent deliberative spaces (Chadwick; Anderson). Avoid assuming static institutional containers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data, computational, and algorithmic influences
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of big data tools, algorithms, visualization, and computational methods that change how journalists gather, analyze, present, and structure stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider computational journalism as supplementing accountability functions (Hamilton & Turner), and evaluate how algorithms and analytics influence routines, audience tailoring, story structure, and metrics-driven decisions. Distinguish data journalism, computational journalism, and CAR (Coddington, 2014).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological multimodality: ethnography and network analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A multimethod approach combining ethnographic (newsroom and network ethnography) observation with quantitative and network analysis to locate actors and understand distributed production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply network ethnography to select sites via social network analysis (Howard, 2002); combine close observation with hypothesis-testing and big-data approaches to capture both micropractices and large-scale patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor-network / technology as integrated practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical perspective treating technology not as exogenous but as integrated into media practice and social relations (actor-network theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how technological affordances and human actors co-constitute routines and organizational behavior; treat tools, processes, and ways of thinking as part of practice rather than outside forces (Latour; Turner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power dynamics and multilevel interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Attention to hierarchical power (including state power) and the interactions across levels—structure vs. agency—and the possibility of multi-directional influence rather than one-way flows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine where power is concentrated and how assemblies and policy-making networks create microspheres of influence (Entman, Bennett, Davis). Study both top-down and bottom-up linkages and how networks mediate or reproduce power relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification, transparency, and second-order newswork
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices related to verifying aggregated/secondhand content, transparency of sourcing and methodologies, and routines that support trustworthy aggregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate news aggregators’ routines for verification and transparency (Coddington, 2015); consider professional ethos versus new screenwork practices and how openness (open-source ethos) influences journalistic norms.
